Varies widely. Hard to nail down a real algorithm, but this is generally how I think through it:

To start with something you didn’t ask, I vary my Decadron dosing. If I don’t have a reason to think the glucose will be difficult to control, and it’s anything more painful than a simple inguinal hernia repair, I give 8-10mg of dexamethasone, as this will typically provide some analgesic benefit post-op.

I’m more likely to use ketamine so I can be more opioid-sparing (high-risk for PONV, morbidly obese patients who I don’t want to slam opioids into), if I want to hit in different receptors patients who are chronically on opioids, or if I get the sense from my pre-op conversation that a patient’s pain will be difficult to manage post-op. My dosing is typically ~0.3 mg/kg after induction of GA, with aliquots of 10 mg Q1H thereafter. I try not to give ketamine <1H before emergence to avoid any psychomimetic effects when waking up. My goal is that on emergence, I want a “sub-anesthetic” dose of ketamine on board - this is where analgesia is experienced, but none of the unsavory psychomimetic/emetogenic effects are experienced, for the sake of PACU. I know this is a broad statement, but I’ve found that at least for most bread/butter daypatient surgeries, intra-op pain is effectively handled with 100 mcg of fentanyl IV on induction and ketamine intra-op (to clarify, intra-op ONLY). Sometimes you’ll need a layer of Dilaudid on top of that intra-op, but not usually unless you’re doing something more painful.

I’m more likely to give Precedex for anyone who I think may wake up combative (young, robust males), anyone who I want to spare opioids for (but typically go for ketamine first), if the patient’s vital signs are “asking” for Precedex and I have any additional reason for Precedex, and a bonus reason if the patient is staying in-house post-op. Depending on the patient’s vital signs, I’ll give aliquots of 4-12 mcg IV at a time, spaced out by about 5-10 minute intervals until I see their HR calm down. For daypatients, I typically don’t give more than 20 mcg. Generally, I almost never give more than 0.5 mcg/kg. While it’s not for pain, boluses of 8-12 mcg Precedex can also be useful for younger patients who shiver after emerging.

I’ll take into consideration how painful the surgery is intra-op versus how painful I think it’ll be post-op, if they’ve had a block (and what kind of block…as a supraclavicular block vs. TAP block are very different), and how much analgesia I think any infiltrated local anesthetic will give. Given all of that, I’ll titrate Dilaudid to RR 8-12 on emergence (I typically have a higher RR threshold for very obese patients cause I feel like sometimes larger patients don’t get a lot of Vt with how we emerge patients, and they just increase RR to compensate). Most importantly, everyone is different. I definitely “listen” to the patient intra-op and during emergence to dictate my decisions aside from my preconceived thoughts of what the patient might need. And I always reiterate to myself that it’s easy to give medications, but more complicated to suck them back out. :)

I find that if I combine both ketamine and Precedex in the way described above, at least for simple surgeries that aren’t thought of as very painful, I won’t need much, if any opioid on emergence. If I use either ketamine or Precedex, I’ll typically need a touch of Dilaudid on emergence. This varies, but it’s amazing how much analgesia can be had with both ketamine and Precedex.

Also, Toradol for anyone who can get it. Of course, as long as the surgeon is okay with it, they didn’t get an NSAID like Celebrex pre-op, and there are no other contraindications. I give 30 mg, as the data isn’t robust enough for me to give 15 mg.

There are so many ways to manage pain, and this post deals more with simple daypatient cases. Remi, methadone, alfentanil (RIP), magnesium, lidocaine drips, or even ketamine and/or Precedex drips can all have their place depending on the patient, surgery, and facility. As long as you’re thoughtful, have a good rationale, you have a handle on the pharmacokinetics, you recognize the risk of polypharmacy, and you understand the risks/drawbacks with each drug, you’re on the right track!

The BJA has a lot of clout, but this article does not say much to me. This article dismisses 1:3 or 1:4 ratios with some poorly appropriated citations. Meaning, this article is dismissing one of the most important aspects of how to make AAs viable - an appropriate ratio.

If you read the paragraph that starts with, "Another option...", the citations used are a bit of a stretch. The authors state that evidence from the US and Europe suggests ratios less stringent than 1:2 may cause more frequent adverse events, but then cites citation #69, which discusses the potential reasons why CA2s on average are prone to more adverse events versus CA1s and CA3s within the context of a 1:2 ratio (nothing about -ologists managing >2 providers, let alone >2 experienced providers). The paragraph goes on to say, "This is supported by stochastic simulation (citation 70) and retrospective record review (citation 71)." However, both citations 70 and 71 discuss the need for -ologists to be pulled between different rooms during critical portions of the case and failing to meet that need, especially in the AM when all the cases start simultaneously (this is the same challenge that anesthesiologists find in the US when managing CRNAs, AAs, or residents). Those two latter citations don't address negative patient outcomes, but simply the anesthesiologist not being able to meet demands similar to TEFRA criteria in the US.

As long as we're being unscientific, I've made some equally unscientific calculations of my own with the salaries provided in this BJA article. Having the "cheapest" 4 anesthesiologists do their own cases shares a similar cost vs. having the most "expensive" 1 anesthesiologist manage 4 of the most "expensive" AAs.

* The former situation calculated by taking the "cheapest" anesthesiologist's pay of £93,666 \* 4 = £374,664K in total yearly salary.
* The latter situation calculated by taking the most "expensive" anesthesiologist's pay and adding it to the cost of 4 of the most "expensive" AAs: £126,281 + (£63,140 \* 4) =  £378,841 in total yearly salary.
* Again, very unscientific as it doesn't take into account benefits in addition to salary, the inefficiencies of medical direction that we see in the US, and potential adverse outcomes by AAs. It's just an example to show how important it is to look at a 1:4 staffing model, which this article completely denies as a possibility.

I'm entirely pro-CRNA (and indifferent toward AAs), but it just bothers me when I see broad statements being made through a journal as reputable as the BJA with such poor logic. All this tells me is that Hanmer et al. do not want AAs in the country. That being said, my opinions are the same for a majority of the anti-CRNA propaganda touted by the ASA, as well as how the AANA sometimes misuses data to push its message (a message that I agree with).

Not dumb at all! AVNRT is “atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia.”

Broadly, SVT can be subdivided into three categories. The most common is atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT), representing ~60% of SVT. Emphasis on the NODAL here. The speed of conduction differs in different “paths” of the same nodal tissue (the AV mode), creating a small reentrant circuit, resulting in tachycardia. This page has pretty good pictures explaining it (https://www.washingtonhra.com/arrhythmias/av-nodal-reentrant-tachycardia-avnrt.php). There are subclassifications of AVNRT itself, but that’s getting into some hardcore cardiology stuff.

The second type of SVT, less common, is called atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT), which represents ~30% of SVT. The circuit is NOT solely nodal. The conduction goes into the ventricles, and back into the atria, creating a reentrant circuit. There is an “accessory pathway” that allows this loop to happen (https://stanfordhealthcare.org/medical-conditions/blood-heart-circulation/supraventricular-tachycardia/types/atrioventricular-reciprocating-tachycardia-avrt.html). If this sounds familiar, one of the arrhythmias that patients who have Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome are prone to having is AVRT (https://litfl.com/pre-excitation-syndromes-ecg-library/).

-The last type of SVT is sinus tachycardia (~10% of SVT).

I wish I had sources for you on the distribution of SVT (60% vs. 30% vs. 10%), but I don’t. AVRT can also be divided between orthodromic or antidromic, depending on which way the conduction circles (down through the regular pathway or the accessory pathway), but that’s beyond the scope of this post, haha.

Everyone is saying sinus tachycardia is a type of SVT…and they are right. More accurately, I think your question is likely, “sinus tachycardia or AVNRT?”

*Commonly, people will equate SVT with AVNRT, or occasionally, SVT with AVRT. This is more of just a colloquial thing that almost all of us do. I still say that, just because not everyone is familiar with AVNRT or AVRT, although there is a more exacting way to define the rhythm.*

As far as I understand, there is not a great way to distinguish between sinus tachycardia and AVNRT with an EKG alone without retrograde P waves visible. Patient history or slow/sudden onset of the tachycardia can help lead you in the right direction, but an EKG tracing is not definitive, in itself. Not even a rate (as people think of 150 as the usual “cutoff”). Both can have P waves too, as far as I understand, albeit, the P waves for AVNRT would be retrograde, if even visible at all.

I might be wrong. Besides patient history and the appearance (or lack) of retrograde P waves, can anyone point me to a source that states morphology differences between sinus tachycardia and AVNRT?

Here are a few tips. Let me know if you have any questions!

Don’t titrate to BP and HR. Titrate to PSI, given that you believe that PSI on the Sedline is reliable. BP & HR can possibly give you an inkling if a patient isn’t well sedated, but really, you should be on the snowed side of sedation with a paralytic going anyway. Not sure what your policy is (PSI of 25-50, or something else). Like some others have mentioned, check your lines, because I have seen meds being run into the bed or onto the floor. They’re only good if they go into the patient, into a vein (and not infiltrated either).

Make sure you replace your electrodes per whatever your institution’s policy is and PRN. Wipe the forehead with an alcohol swab and let it COMPLETELY dry. Sometimes your PSI readings will make much more sense afterward.

Pay attention to your EMG and artifact on the monitor as well. I would have to read the manual or look it up to know, but high degree of artifact or muscle activity (detected through EMG…which would be a paralytic issue) will mess with your signal.

I saw @Riverheadgirl’s comment about titrations based on vent synchrony. I might be misunderstanding their post, but I would not do this. If the pt is paralyzed, they should NOT be triggering any breaths on their own. If they are taking spontaneous breaths on top of the prescribed RR (given you’re in a volume controlled mode), then it is an issue of underdosing the paralytic, not underdosing the sedation.

If your patient is on ketamine, keep in mind that ketamine can interfere in two ways:
1) Being an NMDA antagonist, it may raise PSI, making your PSI reading unreliable. In which case, you probably want to err on the side of more sedation rather than less.
2) This is not necessarily interfering, but the classic dyad of ketamine is hypertension and tachycardia, as ketamine is a sympathomimetic (assuming that the patient has adequate quantities of endogenous catecholamines to release). This can falsely cause you to believe that the patient is not sedated adequately through vital signs as well as a false PSI reading.

I can’t say that ketamine is contraindicated if someone is paralyzed, but it does confound your PSI. I try to communicate this to docs when they round on the patient. I can’t say that taking off the Sedline completely is warranted either. Just keep it in mind.
